narrative.headline: Day 1 checkpoint: 31 components inventoried (16 with known vulnerabilities) and 41 findings, 25 of them introduced by commit 8cad42e — a "routine dependency refresh" from a first-time author that adds malicious typosquats, an unsafe install script, unpinned CI components and a redirected lodash source.
narrative.what_is_in_the_app: sscg-demo-target is a polyglot application with 31 components: 25 packages (13 direct, 12 transitive, max depth 2) spanning npm (7), PyPI (10), Maven (8), GitHub Actions (3), URL-pinned artefacts (2) and Docker (1). The apps are a Node service (acme-orders, package.json), a Java module (com.acme:notifier, notifier/pom.xml), a Python worker (worker/requirements.txt), a Dockerfile and one CI workflow (.github/workflows/ci.yml). 26 components are production scope, 4 CI and 1 dev; the lookup (OSV.dev) reports 16 vulnerable components and 141 advisories.
narrative.what_changed: Commit 8cad42e ("chore: routine dependency refresh", author fastbuilds42, first-time contributor) modified the CI workflow, Dockerfile, package.json/package-lock.json and worker/requirements.txt, and added scripts/setup.js. Added items include fastbuilds42/node:latest, fastbuilds42/cache-helper@main, crossenv@7.0.3, python3-dateutil@2.8.1, urllib3@2.8.0 and two downloaded shell scripts from get.example.invalid; lodash stays at 4.17.15 but its lockfile entry changed. 25 of the 41 findings are new in this change, and 21 findings are Critical overall.
narrative.what_appears_risky: The change bundles supply-chain indicators rather than a dependency refresh: two names flagged as typosquats of popular packages (crossenv vs cross-env, python3-dateutil vs python-dateutil — F-004, F-006, F-012, F-013), a newly added postinstall script that shells out, reads env secrets, base64-hides data and fingerprints the host (F-001), and a lodash pin whose version is unchanged while resolved/integrity now point at npm-mirror.example.invalid (F-005, F-020, F-021). The CI pipeline compounds this: a pull_request_target workflow checking out PR code (F-002), NPM_TOKEN passed to a downloaded script (F-003), curl-to-shell in both CI and the Dockerfile (F-014, F-017), write-all token permissions (F-016) and an unpinned third-party action (F-015), plus an unverified base image from a personal namespace (F-019). Independently of the commit, long-standing vulnerable dependencies remain, including log4j-core@2.14.1 (F-007) and jackson-databind@2.9.8 with 60 advisories (F-008). The triage agent assessed F-018 as suspicious, noting a first-time author changed six build/dependency files under a message that understates the change.

top_concerns.why: A newly added postinstall script that runs shell commands, enumerates credential-shaped env vars, base64-hides its destination and fingerprints the host is the most direct execution path in the change.
crossenv@7.0.3 is a documented malicious package newly added to the dependency set, and it is also flagged as a typosquat (F-012) and as carrying an install script (F-041 per triage).
lodash@4.17.15 keeps the same requested version while its lockfile resolved URL and integrity hash were rewritten — content substitution flagged by three separate rules (F-005, F-020, F-021).

A pull_request_target workflow that checks out the pull request's own code, combined with write-all permissions (F-016) and NPM_TOKEN passed to a downloaded script (F-003), exposes CI secrets and the repo to untrusted PR input.
python3-dateutil@2.8.1 is flagged as a documented malicious typosquat added as a direct production pin alongside the unattributed urllib3@2.8.0 addition (triage F-034/F-035).

caveats: All risk statements are drawn from the evidence packet's findings and inventory; no package versions, CVE or GHSA identifiers beyond those in the packet were verified.

ai_triage verdicts (e.g. on F-001, F-012, F-013, F-018, F-019, F-020, F-021 and on finding IDs such as F-031 through F-041 that have no matching entry in `findings`) are the triage agent's inference, not confirmed evidence.
Several triage rationales reference finding IDs (F-031, F-033, F-034, F-035, F-039, F-041) that are absent from the findings list, so those components are only partially corroborated here.
F-005 shows lodash as "changed" with an identical before/after version string; the packet does not show the actual hash values, so the substitution claim rests on the rule descriptions.
The inventory counts (31 components, 41 findings, 25 new) are internally inconsistent in places (e.g. 16 vulnerabilities vs 25 vulnerability-typed findings) and were reported as given.

F-001.rationale: scripts/setup.js combines several high-signal behaviours in one newly added file: child_process is imported (F-001/E1), credential-shaped env vars are enumerated (F-001/E2), the destination is hidden behind base64 (F-001/E3, F-001/E5), and host/user fingerprinting is collected (F-001/E4). The commit that introduced it comes from a first-time author with a single commit, labelled 'chore: routine dependency refresh', yet it also adds many new components and changes CI/Docker files (F-001/T2) — the classic packaging of an install-time payload behind an innocuous message. The inline comment claiming the file is a 'demo fixture - INERT, never executed, makes no network call' is text written into the scanned code and cannot be taken as proof of safety (F-001/T1); it is in fact identical to the behaviour the code implements. What keeps this below malicious is that no exfiltration call is visible in the excerpted code and the decoded endpoint is a non-routable .invalid host (F-001/E5), so the payload's effectiveness is unproven. Policy also blocks unreviewed install scripts, and this file is not an allow-listed case.
benign_explanations: Legitimate build/setup script that shells out to tooling and reads CI-related environment variables
A deliberately crafted scanner test fixture committed to exercise detection rules
Telemetry/diagnostics bootstrap that only reports host presence, with a placeholder .invalid endpoint
F-001.recommended_next_step: Have a reviewer inspect the full scripts/setup.js (especially lines after the excerpt) for the network send, confirm whether package.json wires it as postinstall, and validate the provenance of author 'fastbuilds42' and the unrelated components added in commit 8cad42e.

F-012.rationale: The dependency name 'crossenv' is one separator edit away from the popular 'cross-env' (F-012/E2) and was added in package.json:18 by a first-time author in a commit titled 'routine dependency refresh' that also introduced several unrelated components (F-012/E1, F-012/T3). Registry metadata shows the name now resolves to an npm security-holding package with one maintainer, four versions and no real repository (F-012/T1), which is consistent with a typosquat that was taken down rather than a legitimate fork. Graph context links this exact component to a documented-malicious finding and an install script flagged elsewhere (F-012/T2), matching the crossenv typosquat campaign pattern. No benign claim (fork, long-standing dependency) is supported: the package is new in this change and has no active repository.
benign_explanations: A legitimate fork or scoped variant of cross-env — rejected: the registry entry points at npm's security-holder placeholder repository, not an active upstream.
A long-standing dependency that predates the change — rejected: graph context shows it is new in this change at depth 1.
F-012.recommended_next_step: Treat the change as compromised: have a human review commit 8cad42e and the first-time author, inspect scripts/setup.js and the other components added in the same commit, and check any environment variables or credentials exposed by the install-script run before reverting the dependency.

F-013.rationale: 'python3-dateutil' resolves to the same string as the popular 'python-dateutil' once separators and prefixes are stripped (F-013/E2), and the PyPI lookup shows no such public package exists at all (F-013/T1) — a name that only makes sense as an imitation. It was added as a direct prod dependency in the latest change (F-013/E1, F-013/T2) by a first-time author whose single 'routine dependency refresh' commit also introduced multiple other new components (F-013/T3). Decisively, the same component is already tracked under a documented malicious package rule (F-006, via F-013/T2) and as an unexpected new prod dependency (F-034), which the typosquat playbook treats as a confirming signal rather than coincidence. No benign explanation (fork, scoped variant with real repository) holds, since there is no registry entry or repository behind the name.
benign_explanations: A private mirror or internal package published only inside the organisation's own index
A typo in an internal requirements name that was never validated against the registry
F-013.recommended_next_step: Have a human review the full commit 8cad42e, the newly added scripts/setup.js and CI/Dockerfile changes, and confirm whether the worker build ever resolves this dependency from a private index; treat the author account and all newly added components from that commit as one incident.

F-018.rationale: A first-time author (F-018/E1) touched CI, Dockerfile, both dependency manifests, the lockfile and added scripts/setup.js in a single commit labelled "chore: routine dependency refresh" (F-018/E2, F-018/T1) — the message understates the change, one of the playbook's confirming signals. The same change introduces a personal Docker image (fastbuilds42/node:latest), an unpinned reference to fastbuilds42/cache-helper@main, remote shell bootstrap/agent scripts from get.example.invalid, and names that mirror legitimate packages (F-018/T1), i.e. exactly the 'new dependency + lockfile + untrusted image + CI change' cluster the playbook says confirms this rule. Provenance is weak: a single commit from an unknown author, no review record, and no repository context to inspect because the finding carries no file location (F-018/T2) and no component metadata (F-018/T3). Nothing in the packet shows actual malicious code or a documented malicious package, so the bar for likely_malicious is not met.
benign_explanations: A new team member making a genuine, reviewed dependency refresh — but no reviewer approval is present and the commit message minimises a large multi-file build change.
An automated dependency bot (dependabot/renovate) — ruled out because the author is a human-style identity with first_time_author=true, not a known bot identity.
Legitimate internal tooling images/scripts under the fastbuilds42 name — weakened by unpinned @main reference and scripts hosted on an unrelated external domain.
F-018.recommended_next_step: Have a second reviewer (per change_management policy) inspect the full diff of 8cad42e: read scripts/setup.js, the ci.yml and Dockerfile edits, confirm who owns the fastbuilds42 registry namespace, inspect the lockfile/resolved-integrity change, and verify the external bootstrap/ci-agent scripts and the added package names against the public registry before merge.

F-019.rationale: The Dockerfile now pulls its base image from a personal namespace, docker.io/fastbuilds42/node:latest (F-019/E1), and the registry lookup shows that namespace/repository does not exist publicly (F-019/T1). The commit that introduced it (F-019/T2) comes from a first-time author whose name matches the image namespace, was labelled a 'routine dependency refresh', and simultaneously added other untrusted artefacts, including a mutable branch reference and scripts fetched from an external host, which weakens any innocent explanation. The related mutable-tag finding on the same component and the policy requirement for digest pinning and trusted publishers both line up with the playbook's confirming indicators for AP-09.
benign_explanations: The image could be an internally mirrored base image kept in a private registry under the author's own namespace and therefore invisible to the public Docker Hub lookup.
The author may be a new team member legitimately performing a dependency refresh, with the image to be published later.
F-019.recommended_next_step: Ask the commit author whether fastbuilds42/node is a sanctioned private image, confirm with the registry/owner that it exists and what it contains, and check the accompanying CI and setup-script changes in the same commit before allowing the build to use it.

F-020.rationale: The lockfile pins lodash@4.17.15 to https://npm-mirror.example.invalid/lodash/-/lodash-4.17.15.tgz (F-020/E1), a host that is not among the policy registries and no corporate mirror is declared, so the playbook's false-positive explanation (a sanctioned Artifactory/Nexus/Verdaccio proxy) does not fit. The same entry's resolved source and integrity hash changed while package.json still requests the same version (F-020/T2, F-005, F-021), which is the lockfile-injection signature of a lockfile-only edit redirecting a known package to a third-party tarball. The change was made by a first-time author in a commit labelled a routine dependency refresh that also bundles unrelated new components such as fastbuilds42 images, crossenv, and remote bootstrap/ci-agent scripts from get.example.invalid (F-020/T1), which weakens any innocent explanation. Nothing in the packet documents the tarball itself as malicious, so this stays at suspicious rather than likely_malicious.
benign_explanations: The host could be an internal npm proxy or mirror used by the organisation, but the policy lists no corporate mirrors for npm.
A developer could have intentionally pointed the lockfile at a build-cache/CDN copy of the identical tarball, yet the integrity hash changed along with the source.
The commit message claims a routine dependency refresh, but that text is not evidence of safety given the unrelated components added in the same commit.
F-020.recommended_next_step: Have a reviewer compare the previous lockfile entry (base commit bf0e651) with the new resolved URL and integrity hash, and inspect the wider change set (scripts/setup.js, Dockerfile, ci.yml, worker/requirements.txt) before any install from that host is permitted.

F-021.rationale: The manifest pins lodash 4.17.15 identically in both commits (F-021/E1), yet the lockfile entry was rewritten so 'resolved' points to npm-mirror.example.invalid instead of registry.npmjs.org and the integrity hash changed (F-021/E2, F-021/T2) — content substitution for an unchanged version, not a semver-driven update, so the npm update/dedupe and lockfile-format false-positive patterns do not apply. The change was made by a first-time author in a single commit labelled 'chore: routine dependency refresh' that also touches CI, the Dockerfile, a new scripts/setup.js, and adds fastbuilds42/node:latest, fastbuilds42/cache-helper@main, crossenv, and downloader URLs (F-021/E3, F-021/T1), which fits lockfile injection far better than innocent maintenance. The same component is independently flagged for an untrusted source, a content-hash mismatch and known vulnerabilities (F-005, F-020, F-025), reinforcing that the mirror redirect is meaningful rather than cosmetic. No benign rationale is offered anywhere in the packet, and the commit message's 'routine' wording is a claim, not evidence.
benign_explanations: A corporate npm mirror was introduced intentionally, but the policy lists no corporate mirrors and the integrity hash changed alongside the host, so the tarball is not the same artifact
An npm update/dedupe or lockfile-format upgrade could rewrite the entry, but the version did not move and neither the host nor the hash pattern stayed normal
The package.json change could be an intentional lodash bump, but the manifest is identical in both commits
F-021.recommended_next_step: Human reviewer should fetch and diff the tarball served by npm-mirror.example.invalid against the registry.npmjs.org artifact for lodash 4.17.15, inspect scripts/setup.js plus the new CI/Docker download URLs, check whether 8cad42e was merged or only pushed, and treat the mirror host and the fastbuilds42/crossenv additions as indicators of the same intrusion.

F-031.rationale: F-031/E1 and F-031/T1 show a new 'postinstall' hook running scripts/setup.js in a package that is not on the policy install-script allow-list, so it is blocked by default and its content is not visible in the packet. F-031/T4 shows it was introduced in commit 8cad42e by a first-time author ('fastbuilds42', author_commit_count 1) under a 'routine dependency refresh' message, in the same change that added a typosquat-style package (crossenv@7.0.3), remote scripts from get.example.invalid, and edits to the CI workflow and Dockerfile — a cluster consistent with a hijacked/compromised contribution path rather than a routine app lifecycle script. The description string 'SSCG demo target - do not install' in F-031/T1 is authored text in the scanned repo and is not treated as evidence of safety. The setup.js body is not shown and no registry/graph data exists for this component (F-031/T2, F-031/T3), so the script itself could not be confirmed malicious, keeping this below likely_malicious.
benign_explanations: Application's own lifecycle script that only builds or copies local files (playbook false-positive pattern), though it would be new rather than pre-existing and was added by an unfamiliar author
A legitimate setup/bootstrap step the maintainer intended for the service, whose content is simply not visible in this packet
F-031.recommended_next_step: Inspect scripts/setup.js in commit 8cad42e and the changes to .github/workflows/ci.yml and Dockerfile, confirm whether the script downloads/executes remote content or reads environment variables/credentials, verify the identity of author 'fastbuilds42' and the provenance of the newly added components (crossenv, get.example.invalid scripts, fastbuilds42/* images), and hold deployment until then.

F-033.rationale: F-033/T3 records that this exact component already carries a documented-malicious finding (F-004), a typosquat finding against the popular 'cross-env' (F-012) and an uninspected install script (F-041), so the new dependency is not an isolated event. F-033/T2 shows the registry entry is a 'security holding package' whose latest published version is 0.0.2-security and whose pinned version is not actually present in the registry (this_version_in_registry: false), consistent with a name that was taken over after abuse rather than a genuine 7.0.3 release. F-033/T1 shows the addition came from a first-time author in a single commit that also pulled in an unpinned personal Docker image, a @main helper, remote bootstrap/ci-agent scripts and an inconsistent lodash resolution, while the message only says 'chore: routine dependency refresh'. The playbook confirms this pattern: an unexplained new direct dependency from a first-time contributor that overlaps with typosquat and install-script rules.
benign_explanations: A developer genuinely wanted a cross-platform env-var helper and mistyped the well-known 'cross-env' package name
The dependency is dev-scope only and might not run in production
F-033.recommended_next_step: Treat crossenv@7.0.3 as compromised: confirm whether it was ever installed or executed in CI or developer machines, review the commit 8cad42e changes to .github/workflows/ci.yml, the Dockerfile and scripts/setup.js for the paired payload, and verify how package-lock.json resolved a version that the registry does not list.

F-034.rationale: The added production pin python3-dateutil==2.8.1 (F-034/E1) is for a name that does not exist on PyPI at all, so it cannot be resolved from the public registry (F-034/T2), and the graph context records it as a documented malicious package and as a typosquat of the popular 'python-dateutil' (F-034/T3, F-006, F-013). It arrived in a first-time author's single commit labelled 'chore: routine dependency refresh' (F-034/E2, F-034/T1), which bundles unrelated CI, Dockerfile and install-script changes plus other untrusted components — the routine message is a claim, not evidence of safety. The playbook's confirm indicators apply: the commit message does not justify the dependency, the author is a first-time contributor, another rule overlaps (typosquat/no real repository), and it is a prod dependency of a network-facing worker. This matches typosquatting of a popular package.
benign_explanations: A legitimate but privately hosted fork of python-dateutil misnamed in requirements.txt — weakened because the registry lookup found no such package and a typosquat rule fired on the same name (F-034/T2, F-034/T3)
A routine dependency refresh by a new maintainer — weakened by the unrelated bundle of CI, Dockerfile and bootstrap-script changes in the same commit (F-034/T1)
F-034.recommended_next_step: Human reviewer (incident response) should verify the provenance of the python3-dateutil pin and the other components introduced in commit 8cad42e (including the added setup script and CI/workflow edits), and treat the dependency as untrusted until confirmed.

F-035.rationale: urllib3 itself is a long-established, real PyPI package (first upload 2009, 109 releases, 2.8.0 not yanked — F-035/T2), so the package name is not the problem. The problem is the change: a first-time author with a single commit ('chore: routine dependency refresh' — F-035/E2, F-035/T1) added an unpinned urllib3 line (F-035/E1, F-035/T4), which violates the exact-pin policy, and bundled it with several unrelated and far riskier additions in the same commit (unknown registry images, a crossenv package, and scripts fetched from an external host — F-035/T1). An innocent dependency refresh is weakened by that combination, though nothing in the packet shows urllib3@2.8.0 behaving maliciously.
benign_explanations: requests is already a direct dependency (F-035/T4), so urllib3 could be added deliberately as its HTTP backend or for direct connection-pool use
A routine dependency refresh by a developer legitimately updating the worker's requirements
Version 2.8.0 is a genuine, current, non-yanked PyPI release of a well-known library (F-035/T2)
F-035.recommended_next_step: Have a reviewer inspect the whole commit 8cad42e, not just this line: confirm who 'fastbuilds42' is, why urllib3 was added unpinned while the rest of the file is pinned, and what the co-added images, crossenv entry, setup.js and externally fetched scripts do before merging.

F-039.rationale: worker/requirements.txt pins every other dependency exactly (requests==2.19.1, PyYAML==5.3, Jinja2==2.10, python3-dateutil==2.8.1) but leaves urllib3 with no version at all (F-039/E1, F-039/T2), violating the organisation's python_exact_pins policy so builds can silently resolve any future release. The change that introduced it (F-039/T3) comes from a first-time author with a single commit, disguised as a 'chore: routine dependency refresh', and bundles unrelated high-risk additions such as fastbuilds42/node:latest, fastbuilds42/cache-helper@main, crossenv@7.0.3 and get.example.invalid install scripts. That combination of an unpinned production dependency with an unreviewed, unusually broad first-time contribution makes an innocent explanation weaker than the risk indicators. This is judged by behaviour and provenance, not by the reassuring commit message.
benign_explanations: Libraries that intentionally declare ranges and are always installed from a lockfile (playbook false-positive pattern) — weakened here because Python requirements are the only pinning mechanism visible and all sibling entries are exactly pinned.
A routine automated dependency-refresh bot — weakened because the author is a first-time contributor and the same commit touches CI, Dockerfile, package.json and adds setup.js.
F-039.recommended_next_step: Have a human review the whole commit 8cad42e, especially who 'fastbuilds42' is, the provenance of the added container images and get.example.invalid scripts, the crossenv@7.0.3 entry (possible typosquat of cross-env), and whether a Python lockfile or hash pinning exists before merging.

F-041.rationale: The lockfile confirms crossenv@7.0.3 declares an install script (F-041/E1), and the registry record for the name shows only a 'security holding package' placeholder repo (git+https://github.com/npm/security-holder.git) with this version absent from the registry (F-041/T2) — the fingerprint of a package removed for abuse rather than a functioning build tool. The graph context reports the same component is independently flagged as a documented malicious package (F-004), as a typosquat of 'cross-env' (F-012), and as a newly added dev dependency (F-033) per F-041/T3, so the install-script alert is not an isolated heuristic hit. The name is one edit away from the popular 'cross-env', with an install script and no genuine repository, matching the documented crossenv typosquat family (AP-01). No innocent explanation (native build step, hook installer, telemetry) fits, and the package is not on the install-script allow-list; any 'routine dependency refresh' framing in the commit message is not evidence of safety.
benign_explanations: Legitimate native build or prebuild step requiring an install script
A local lifecycle/build helper that only copies or compiles local files
F-041.recommended_next_step: Confirm removal of crossenv@7.0.3 from the lockfile/package.json, and review the scripts/setup.js added in the same commit (8cad42e) plus any CI runs that installed this dependency for credential exposure; escalate to incident response.
